verses.text: A man named Job lived in the land of Uz. He was blameless and upright, revered God, and turned away from evil.
He had seven sons and three daughters.

He owned seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred teams of oxen, and five hundred female donkeys. He had a very large household and was the most prominent man among all the people of the east.
Each of his sons held a feast at his own house on his birthday. They invited their three sisters to eat and drink with them.

When the days of feasting were over, Job would send for his children and consecrate them. He'd get up early and present a burnt offering for each one. He thought, "Maybe my children have sinned and turned against God in their hearts." Job made a practice of this.
One day the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan came with them.
The LORD asked Satan, "Where have you come from?" Satan replied, "From roaming back and forth across the earth and walking all over it."
The LORD asked Satan, "Have you paid attention to my servant Job? There's no one like him on earth. He's blameless and upright, reveres God, and turns away from evil."
Satan answered, "Does Job fear God for nothing?
Haven't you put a hedge around him, his household, and everything he owns? You've blessed his work, and his possessions have spread across the land.
Reach out and strike everything he owns, and he'll turn against you to your face."
The LORD told Satan, "Everything he owns is in your power. Keep your hand off Job himself." Then Satan left the LORD's presence.
One day Job's sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine at their oldest brother's house.
A messenger came to Job and said, "The oxen were plowing and the donkeys were grazing beside them
when the Sabeans attacked and took them. They killed the servants with the sword. I'm the only one who escaped to tell you."
While he was still speaking, another messenger came and said, "The fire of God fell from the sky and burned up the sheep and the servants. I'm the only one who escaped to tell you."

While he was still speaking, another came and said, "The Chaldeans divided into three groups, swept down on the camels, and took them. They killed the servants with the sword. I'm the only one who escaped to tell you."
While he was still speaking, another came and said, "Your sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine at their oldest brother's house.
Suddenly a powerful wind came from the wilderness and struck all four corners of the house. It collapsed on them, and they're dead. I'm the only one who escaped to tell you."
Job stood up, tore his robe, and shaved his head. Then he fell to the ground and worshiped.
He said, "I came naked from my mother's womb, and I'll leave this life naked. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away. May the LORD's name be blessed."
Through all of this Job neither sinned nor accused God of wrongdoing.
On another day the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan came with them to stand before the LORD.
The LORD asked Satan, "Where have you come from?" Satan answered, "From roaming back and forth across the earth and walking all over it."

The LORD said, "Have you paid attention to my servant Job? There's no one like him on earth. He's blameless and upright, reveres God, and turns away from evil. He still holds on to his integrity, even though you urged me to ruin him for no reason."
Satan answered the LORD, "Skin for skin! A person will give up everything to save their own life.
Reach out now and strike his bones and flesh, and he'll turn against you to your face."
The LORD told Satan, "He's in your power. Spare his life."
Satan left the LORD's presence and struck Job with painful sores from the soles of his feet to the top of his head.
Job picked up a piece of broken pottery to scrape his skin while he sat in the ashes.
His wife asked him, "Are you still holding on to your integrity? Renounce God and die."
Job told her, "You're talking like a foolish woman. Should we accept good from God and refuse to accept trouble?" Through all this, Job said nothing sinful.

When Job's three friends heard about the disasters that had come upon him, they each set out from home. Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite agreed to go together to share his grief and comfort him.
When they saw him from a distance, they barely recognized him. They wept aloud, tore their robes, and threw dust into the air over their heads.
They sat on the ground with him for seven days and seven nights. No one said a word to him because they could see how deeply he was suffering.
After this Job finally spoke and cursed the day he was born.
This is what Job said:
"May the day I was born disappear, and the night that announced, 'A boy has been conceived.'
May that day go dark. May God above take no notice of it. May no light shine on it.
Let darkness and the shadow of death claim it. Let a cloud settle on it, and let everything that blackens the day terrify it.
Let thick darkness take that night. Let it have no place among the days of the year and never be counted among the months.
Let that night be barren. Let no voice of joy be heard in it.
Let those who curse days curse that night, those who are ready to rouse Leviathan.
Let its morning stars go dark. Let it wait for light that never comes and never see the first glimmer of dawn,
because it failed to close my mother's womb and hide this suffering from my eyes.
Why didn't I die at birth? Why didn't I breathe my last when my mother brought me into the world?
Why were there knees to receive me and breasts to nurse me?
By now I'd be lying still and quiet. I'd be asleep and at rest,
with the kings and advisers of the earth who rebuilt ruins for themselves,
or with rulers who had gold and filled their houses with silver.
Or I'd never have been here, like a stillborn child hidden away, like babies who never saw daylight.
There the wicked stop causing trouble, and there the weary find rest.
Prisoners are at ease together there. They no longer hear the voice of the one who drove them.
The least and the greatest are both there, and the slave is free from his master.
Why give light to someone in misery, or life to people whose souls are bitter,
who long for death that never comes and search for it more eagerly than for buried treasure,
who would be overjoyed and celebrate if they found the grave?
Why give light to a man who can't see where he's going, a man God has fenced in?
I sigh instead of eating, and my groans pour out like water.
What I dreaded has happened to me. The thing I feared has come upon me.
I have no peace, no quiet, no rest. All I have is trouble."
Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered:
"Will it upset you if someone tries to speak to you? Still, who could hold back from speaking?
Think of how many people you've taught and how often you've strengthened weak hands.
Your words held up people who were about to fall. You steadied knees that were giving way.
Now trouble has come to you, and you're losing heart. It touches you, and you're shaken.
Isn't reverence for God your confidence? Isn't the integrity of your life your hope?
Think back. Who ever died while innocent? Where have upright people been cut down?
From what I've seen, people who plow wrongdoing and sow trouble harvest what they've planted.
At God's breath they perish. The blast of his anger consumes them.
The lion's roar and the fierce lion's growl fall silent, and the young lions' teeth are broken.
The old lion dies for lack of prey, and the lioness's cubs scatter.
A word came to me in secret. My ear caught a whisper of it.
As thoughts stirred from visions in the night, when people fall into deep sleep,
fear and trembling came over me and shook me to the bones.
A spirit passed in front of me, and the hair on my body stood up.
It stood still. I couldn't make out what it looked like, but a shape was right in front of me. After a silence I heard a voice:
'Can a mortal be more just than God? Can anyone be purer than their Maker?
Even his servants don't have his full trust. He finds fault with his angels.
How much more with those who live in houses of clay, founded on dust, and crushed more easily than a moth?
Between morning and evening they're shattered. They disappear forever, and no one pays attention.
Their tent cord is pulled loose. They die without gaining wisdom.'"
"Go ahead and call out. Will anyone answer you? Which of the holy ones will you turn to?
Resentment kills the fool, and jealousy kills the simple.
I've seen a fool take root, but I quickly called his home cursed.
His children are far from safety. They're crushed at the city gate, with no one to rescue them.
The hungry eat up his harvest, taking it even from among the thorns. A trap stands open for everything they own.
Suffering doesn't come out of the dust, and trouble doesn't sprout from the ground.
People are born into trouble as surely as sparks fly upward.
If it were me, I'd seek God and put my case in his hands.
He does great things beyond understanding, more wonders than anyone can count.
He gives rain to the earth and sends water over the fields.
He lifts up those who've been brought low and raises those who mourn to safety.
He ruins the plans of the crafty so they can't carry out what they've set out to do.
He catches the wise in their own schemes, and the plans of the cunning collapse.
They run into darkness in broad daylight and grope at noon as if it were night.
But God rescues the needy from words that cut like swords and from the grip of the powerful.
So the poor have hope, and injustice has to shut its mouth.
Look, how fortunate is the person God corrects. So don't despise the Almighty's discipline.
He wounds, and he dresses the wound. He injures, and his own hands heal.
He'll rescue you from six troubles. Even in seven, no harm will touch you.
In famine he'll save you from death, and in war he'll save you from the sword.
You'll be sheltered from the lash of the tongue, and you won't fear destruction when it comes.
You'll laugh at destruction and famine and won't be afraid of wild animals.
Even the stones in the field will be at peace with you, and the wild animals will leave you unharmed.
You'll know your tent is secure. When you check your fold, nothing will be missing.
You'll see your descendants grow numerous, like the grass of the earth.
You'll come to your grave at a ripe old age, like a bundle of grain gathered in its season.
We've looked into this and found it true. Listen to it and take it to heart for your own good."
Then Job answered:
"If only my anguish could be weighed and all my suffering placed on the scales!
It would weigh more than the sand of the seas. That's why my words have been rash.
The Almighty's arrows are lodged in me, and my spirit drinks their poison. God's terrors line up against me.
Does a wild donkey bray when it has grass? Does an ox bellow when it has feed?
Can you eat bland food without salt? Does the white of an egg have any flavor?
I can't bring myself to touch such things. They're like food that makes me sick.
If only I could have what I've asked for, if only God would grant what I long for,
if only God were willing to crush me, to let his hand loose and cut me off.
Then I'd still have this comfort. Even in pain that won't let up, I could rejoice that I haven't denied the words of the Holy One.
How much strength do I have left to keep waiting? What end can I look forward to that would make me patient?
Am I as strong as stone? Is my body made of bronze?
There's no help left in me. Any resource I had has been driven away.
A person who's about to give up should receive kindness from a friend, even if they've lost their reverence for the Almighty.
My brothers have been as unreliable as a seasonal stream, like channels that run dry.
They're dark with ice and full of melting snow.
Then the dry season comes, and they vanish. In the heat they disappear from their beds.
Caravans turn aside looking for them, go out into the wasteland, and perish.
The caravans from Tema look for them, and the travelers from Sheba wait for them.
They arrive full of confidence and are stunned and distressed.
Now you've turned out to be no help. You see something terrifying and draw back in fear.
Did I ever ask you to give me anything or pay for a gift out of your own wealth?
Did I ask you to rescue me from an enemy or buy my freedom from my oppressors?
Teach me and I'll be quiet. Show me where I've gone wrong.
Honest words can hit hard. But what have your accusations proved?
Are you trying to correct mere words, treating the speech of someone in despair as wind?
You'd even cast lots for an orphan and sell off your own friend.
Now please look at me. I wouldn't lie to your face.
Please reconsider. Don't judge me unfairly. Think again, because my cause is just.
Have I spoken unjustly? Can't I tell the taste of something wrong?"
"Isn't human life on earth a term of hard labor? Aren't our days like those of a hired worker?
Like a servant desperate for shade, like a hired worker waiting for his pay,
I've been given months of misery and assigned nights of weariness.
When I lie down, I ask, 'When can I get up? When will this night end?' I toss and turn until dawn.
My body is covered with worms and clumps of dirt. My skin closes up and then breaks open again.
My days pass faster than a weaver's shuttle and run out without hope.
Remember that my life is just a breath. My eyes won't see good days again.
Those who see me now will see me no more. You'll look for me, but I'll be gone.
As a cloud fades and disappears, so anyone who goes down to Sheol never comes back up.
They'll never return to their home, and the place they belonged to won't know them anymore.
So I won't keep quiet. I'll speak from the anguish in my spirit and complain out of the bitterness of my soul.
Am I the sea or a sea monster that you have to put a guard over me?
When I say, 'My bed will comfort me, and my couch will give me some relief,'
you frighten me with dreams and terrify me with visions.
I'd rather be strangled and die than live in this body.
I hate my life. I don't want to live forever. Leave me alone, because my days are only a breath.
What are human beings that you make so much of them and pay them so much attention,
checking on them every morning and testing them at every moment?
Won't you look away long enough to let me swallow my own spit?
If I've sinned, what have I done to you, watcher of human beings? Why have you made me your target, so I've become a burden to myself?
Why don't you forgive my disobedience and take away my guilt? Soon I'll lie down in the dust. You'll search for me, but I'll be gone."
Then Bildad the Shuhite answered:
"How long will you talk like this? Your words are blowing like a strong wind.
Does God twist justice? Does the Almighty distort what is right?
If your children sinned against him, he handed them over to the consequences of their disobedience.
If you'll seek God earnestly, plead with the Almighty.
If you're pure and upright, he'll surely rise to help you and restore your home to prosperity.
Even if your beginnings were small, your future would be far greater.
Ask the generations who came before us. Find out what their ancestors learned.
We only arrived yesterday and know so little, because our days on earth are a passing shadow.
Won't they teach you and speak to you from what they've learned in their hearts?
Can papyrus grow without a marsh? Can reeds grow without water?
While still green and uncut, they wither faster than any other reed.
That's what happens to everyone who forgets God. The hope of the godless dies away.
Their confidence snaps. What they trust is as fragile as a spider's web.
They lean on their house, but it won't stand. They grab hold of it, but it won't last.
They're like a plant green in the sun, with shoots spreading across the garden.
Its roots wrap around a pile of stones and reach into the rocky ground.
If it's torn out of its place, that place disowns it and says, 'I've never seen you.'
That's all the joy it gets from its course. Other plants spring from the ground in its place.
God won't reject a blameless person, and he won't lend a hand to those who do wrong.
He'll yet fill your mouth with laughter and your lips with shouts of joy.
Those who hate you will be clothed in shame, and the tent of the wicked will disappear."
Then Job answered:
"I know that's true. But how can anyone be in the right before God?
If someone wanted to argue a case with him, they couldn't answer him once in a thousand times.
God is wise and mighty. Who has ever set themselves against him and come out well?
He moves mountains before they know what's happening, overturning them in his anger.
He shakes the earth out of its place, and its pillars tremble.
He orders the sun to stay down and seals up the stars.
He alone stretches out the heavens and walks on the waves of the sea.
He made the Bear, Orion, and the Pleiades, and the hidden regions of the southern sky.
He does great things nobody can fathom, more wonders than anyone can count.
He passes by me, and I don't see him. He moves on, and I don't even notice.
When he takes something away, who can stop him? Who can ask him, 'What are you doing?'
God won't hold back his anger. Even Rahab's helpers bow beneath him.
How much less could I answer him or find the words to argue my case?
Even if I were in the right, I couldn't answer him. I'd have to plead for mercy from my judge.
Even if I called and he answered, I wouldn't believe he was listening to me.
He crushes me with a storm and gives me wound after wound for no reason.
He won't let me catch my breath. He fills me with bitterness.
If this is a contest of strength, he's the mighty one. If it's a matter for the court, he asks, 'Who will summon me?'
Even if I'm in the right, my own mouth will condemn me. Even if I'm blameless, I'll be declared guilty.
I am blameless. I've stopped caring what happens to me. I despise my life.
It all comes to the same thing. That's why I say he destroys both the blameless and the wicked.
When disaster kills without warning, he mocks the distress of the innocent.
The earth is handed over to the wicked, and he covers the eyes of its judges. If it isn't him, then who is it?
My days run faster than a runner. They flee without seeing anything good.
They slip away like swift boats, like an eagle swooping down on its prey.
If I say, 'I'll forget my complaint, take off this sad face, and cheer up,'
I'm still afraid of all my suffering. I know you won't declare me innocent.
I'm going to be condemned, so why wear myself out for nothing?
Even if I wash myself with snow and scrub my hands with lye,
you'll plunge me into a ditch, and even my own clothes will loathe me.
God isn't human like me. I can't answer him as if we could stand together in court.
There's no one to decide between us, no one who could lay a hand on both of us.
If only he would take his rod away from me and stop terrifying me,
then I could speak without being afraid of him. As things stand, I can't."
"I'm worn out by my life. I'll speak my complaint freely and let the bitterness in my soul come out.
I'll say to God, 'Don't condemn me. Show me why you have a case against me.
Does it please you to oppress me, despise what your own hands made, and smile on the plans of the wicked?
Do you have human eyes? Do you see things the way people do?
Are your days as short as a mortal's, or your years like a human lifetime,
that you have to hunt for my guilt and search for my sin?
You know I'm not wicked, yet no one can rescue me from your hand.
Your hands shaped and made every part of me, and now you're destroying me.
Please remember that you shaped me like clay. Will you turn me back into dust?
Didn't you pour me out like milk and let me thicken like cheese?
You clothed me with skin and flesh and knit me together with bones and tendons.
You gave me life and showed me faithful love, and your care kept my spirit alive.
Yet you kept these things hidden in your heart. I know this was in your mind:
if I sinned, you'd take note of it and refuse to clear me of my guilt.
If I'm wicked, I'm doomed. Even if I'm right, I can't lift my head. I'm full of disgrace and all too aware of my suffering.
If I hold my head high, you hunt me like a lion and show your power against me again.
You bring fresh witnesses against me and increase your anger toward me. Wave after wave of trouble comes at me like troops in battle.
Why did you bring me out of the womb? I wish I'd breathed my last before anyone saw me.
It would have been as though I'd never existed, carried straight from the womb to the grave.
Aren't my days few? Stop and leave me alone so I can have a little comfort
before I go where I can't return, to the land of darkness and the shadow of death,
a land dark as midnight, where the shadow of death covers everything and nothing has order, where even the light is like midnight.'"
Then Zophar the Naamathite answered:
"Should all those words go unanswered? Does a flood of talk prove someone right?
Should your boasting silence everyone? Will no one put you to shame when you mock us?
You say, 'What I teach is pure, and I'm clean in your sight.'
If only God would speak and open his mouth to answer you.
If only he'd show you the secrets of wisdom, because true wisdom has more than one side. Then you'd know God is holding you to account for less than your guilt deserves.
Can you get to the bottom of God's mysteries? Can you find the limits of the Almighty?
They're as high as heaven. What can you do? They're deeper than Sheol. What can you know?
They stretch farther than the earth and wider than the sea.
If God passes by, locks someone up, or calls the court into session, who can stand in his way?
He knows who is false. He sees wrongdoing even without having to look for it.
A fool will become wise when a wild donkey gives birth to a human.
If you set your heart right, stretch out your hands to God.
If there's wrongdoing in your hands, put it far from you. Clear injustice out of your tents.
Then you'll be able to lift your face without shame. You'll stand firm and won't be afraid.
You'll forget your misery. You'll remember it only as water that has flowed past.
Your life will be brighter than noon. Even its darkness will be like morning.
You'll feel secure because there's hope. You'll look around and lie down safely.
You'll rest with no one to frighten you, and many people will seek your favor.
But the eyes of the wicked will fail. They won't find a way to escape. Their only hope will be to breathe their last."
Then Job answered:
"Of course, you're the only people who know anything. Wisdom will die when you do.
I have understanding just as you do. I'm not beneath you. Who doesn't know the things you've been saying?
My neighbors laugh at me, even though I used to call on God and he answered me. They laugh at someone who is just and blameless.
People at ease look down on those in trouble. They have contempt ready for anyone whose feet slip.
Robbers live in prosperous tents. Those who provoke God live securely, carrying their god in their own hands.
Ask the animals, and they'll teach you. Ask the birds in the sky, and they'll tell you.
Speak to the earth, and it will teach you. The fish of the sea will tell you too.
Which of them doesn't know that the LORD's hand has done this?
The life of every living creature and the breath of all humanity are in his hand.
Doesn't the ear weigh words as the tongue tastes food?
Wisdom comes with age, and understanding with a long life.
God has wisdom and strength. Good counsel and understanding belong to him.
When he tears something down, no one can rebuild it. When he locks someone up, no one can set them free.
When he holds back the waters, they dry up. When he lets them loose, they overturn the land.
Strength and sound wisdom are his. Both the people who deceive and those they deceive belong to him.
He leads advisers away stripped of what they had and makes fools of judges.
He loosens the bonds imposed by kings and ties a belt around their waists.
He leads priests away stripped of what they had and brings down the powerful.
He silences trusted advisers and takes away the judgment of elders.
He pours contempt on nobles and loosens the belts of the strong.
He uncovers what lies hidden in the dark and brings the shadow of death into the light.
He makes nations grow and then destroys them. He expands their territory and then leads their people away captive.
He takes understanding away from the leaders of the earth and makes them wander in a wilderness with no path.
They grope in darkness without light. He makes them stagger like people who are drunk."
"I've seen all this with my own eyes. I've heard it with my own ears and understood it.
What you know, I know too. I'm not beneath you.
I want to speak to the Almighty himself. I want to argue my case with God.
You cover things up with lies. Every one of you is a useless doctor.
If only you'd keep completely quiet! That would show some wisdom.
Hear my argument now. Listen to the case I'm making.
Will you say things that are wrong on God's behalf? Will you lie for him?
Will you show him favoritism? Will you argue God's case for him?
Will it go well for you if he examines you? Can you fool him the way you fool another person?
He'll surely rebuke you if you secretly show favoritism.
Won't his majesty frighten you? Won't terror of him fall on you?
Your memorable sayings are proverbs made of ash. Your defenses are made of clay.
Quiet! Leave me to speak, whatever happens to me.
Why should I take my flesh in my teeth and put my life in my hands?
He may kill me. I have no hope, but I'll still defend my conduct to his face.
This too will be my salvation, because someone who is godless wouldn't dare come before him.
Listen carefully to what I say. Let my statement sink in.
Look, I've prepared my case. I know I'm in the right.
Who can press a case against me? If someone could, I'd fall silent and breathe my last.
Only grant me two things, and I won't hide from you:
take your hand far away from me, and stop terrifying me.
Then call, and I'll answer. Or let me speak, and you answer me.
How many wrongs and sins have I committed? Show me my rebellion and my sin.
Why do you hide your face and treat me as your enemy?
Would you frighten a leaf blown by the wind or chase after dry stalks?
You write bitter charges against me and make me pay for the wrongs of my youth.
You put my feet in stocks and track every path I take. You set a limit on where I can step,
while I waste away like something rotten, like a piece of clothing eaten by moths.
A person born of a woman has few days, and those days are full of trouble.
Like a flower, they spring up and are cut down. Like a shadow, they slip away and are gone.
Do you fix your eyes on someone so frail and bring me into court with you?
Who can bring something clean out of something unclean? No one.
You've fixed the length of a person's life. You know the number of their months and have set a limit they cannot pass.
Look away and give them some rest until they finish their day, like a hired worker.
Even a tree that has been cut down has hope. It can sprout again and keep sending out tender shoots.
Its roots may grow old in the earth and its stump may die in the ground,
but at the scent of water it buds and puts out branches like a young plant.
But a person dies and lies still. They breathe their last, and where are they?
As water drains from a sea and a river dwindles and dries up,
a person lies down and never gets up. Until the heavens are gone, they won't wake or be stirred from their sleep.
If only you would hide me in Sheol and keep me there until your anger passed! If only you would set a time to remember me!
If a person dies, will they live again? I would wait through all my days of struggle until my release came.
You'd call and I'd answer. You'd long to see what your hands had made.
But now you count my steps. Don't you watch for my sin?
My rebellion is sealed in a bag, and you keep my guilt tied up.
But a mountain falls and crumbles, and a rock is moved from its place.
Water wears down stones, and floods wash away the soil. In the same way you destroy human hope.
You overpower a person for good, and they go away. You change their face and send them away.
If their children rise to honor, they don't know it. If their children are brought low, they don't see it happen.
All they feel is the pain in their own body and the grief within them."
Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered:
"Would a wise person answer with empty ideas and fill himself with the east wind?
Would he argue with useless talk and speeches that do no good?
You undermine reverence for God and discourage devotion to him.
Your guilt tells your mouth what to say, and you choose the words of people who scheme.
Your own mouth condemns you. Your own lips testify against you.
Were you the first person ever born? Did you come into the world before the hills?
Have you listened in on God's private counsel? Do you think wisdom belongs to you alone?
What do you know that we don't? What do you understand that we haven't grasped?
We have gray-haired men and elders among us who are much older than your father.
Is God's comfort too little for you, even when the words spoken to you are gentle?
Why do you let your heart carry you away? Why do your eyes flash,
so that you turn your spirit against God and let these words out of your mouth?
How can a human being be clean? How can anyone born of a woman be righteous?
God doesn't even trust his holy ones. The heavens themselves aren't clean in his sight.
How much less someone corrupt and detestable, someone who drinks wrongdoing like water!
Listen to me and I'll show you. I'll tell you what I've seen,
what wise people learned from their ancestors and passed on without hiding it.
The land was given to those ancestors alone, and no foreigner passed among them.
A wicked person writhes in pain all his days, through all the years set aside for an oppressor.
Terrifying sounds fill his ears. While he's prospering, the destroyer comes upon him.
He doesn't expect to find his way back out of the darkness. A sword waits for him.
He wanders in search of bread, asking, 'Where is it?' He knows the day of darkness is close at hand.
Distress and anguish terrify him and overpower him like a king ready for battle.
He has raised his hand against God and acted arrogantly toward the Almighty.
He charges at God in defiance behind his thick shields.
His face is covered with fat, and his thighs have grown fat.
He has settled in deserted towns, in houses nobody lived in that were ready to collapse into heaps.
He won't stay rich, his wealth won't last, and his possessions won't spread over the land.
He won't escape the darkness. Flames will dry up his branches, and the breath of God's mouth will carry him away.
Let him stop fooling himself by trusting in emptiness. Emptiness is what he'll get in return.
His end will come before his time, and his branches will never turn green.
He'll drop his unripe grapes like a vine and shed his blossoms like an olive tree.
The company of the godless will bear no fruit, and fire will consume the tents of those who take bribes.
They conceive trouble and give birth to wrongdoing. In their hearts they prepare deceit."
Then Job answered:
"I've heard plenty of talk like this. You're all miserable comforters!
Will these empty words ever end? What keeps driving you to answer?
I could talk just like you if our places were reversed. I could string words together against you and shake my head at you.
But I'd use my words to strengthen you. I'd say something that could ease your pain.
When I speak, my grief doesn't ease. When I keep quiet, how does that help?
God, you've worn me out. You've left everyone around me desolate.
You've made me waste away, and that stands as a witness against me. My thin body rises up and testifies to my face.
In his anger he tears at me and hunts me down. He grinds his teeth at me. My enemy fixes his eyes on me.
They open their mouths wide against me, slap my cheek to humiliate me, and gather together against me.
God hands me over to the ungodly and throws me into the hands of the wicked.
I was at peace, and he shattered me. He grabbed me by the neck and dashed me to pieces. Then he set me up as his target.
His archers surround me. He strikes through my kidneys without mercy and spills my bile on the ground.
He breaks through me again and again, charging at me like a giant.
I've sewn sackcloth against my skin and humbled my strength in the dust.
My face is red from crying, and deep darkness hangs over my eyelids,
even though my hands have done no violence and my prayer is pure.
Earth, don't cover my blood. Let my cry find no place to rest.
Even now my witness is in heaven. The one who can speak for me is on high.
My friends mock me, and my eyes pour out tears to God.
If only someone would plead for a person before God, as one person pleads for a neighbor.
In just a few years I'll go down the road from which no one returns.
"My spirit is broken. My days have burned out, and the grave is waiting for me.
Mockers surround me. I have to sit here watching them provoke me.
God, put up a pledge for me yourself. Who else will give me their hand as a guarantee?
You've kept them from understanding, so you won't let them triumph.
Anyone who betrays friends for a share of the spoils will see even their children's eyes fail.
God has made me a byword among the people. They spit in my face.
My eyes have grown dim from grief, and my whole body is a shadow of what it was.
Upright people are appalled at this. The innocent are stirred up against the godless.
Still, the righteous hold to their way, and those with clean hands grow stronger and stronger.
As for all of you, come back and try again. I won't find a single wise person among you.
My days have passed. My plans and the deepest desires of my heart have fallen apart.
They call night day. In the middle of the darkness they say, 'The light is near.'
If I look to Sheol as my home and spread out my bed in the dark,
if I say to decay, 'You're my father,' and to the worm, 'You're my mother and my sister,'
then where is my hope? Who can see any hope for me?
Will it go down with me to the gates of Sheol? Will we go down into the dust together?"
Then Bildad the Shuhite answered:
"How long will you keep hunting for words? Think it through, and then we'll speak.
Why do you treat us like animals and count us unclean?
You tear yourself apart in your anger. Should everyone abandon the earth for your sake? Should the rock be moved out of its place?
The light of the wicked will go out. Their fire won't give off a spark.
The light in their tent will go dark, and the lamp over their heads will be put out.
Their strong strides will become short. Their own plans will bring them down.
Their own feet carry them into a net, and they walk straight into its mesh.
A snare catches them by the heel, and a trap holds them fast.
A noose lies hidden in the ground and a trap in their path.
Terrors frighten them from every side and chase at their heels.
Their strength wastes away, and disaster waits beside them.
Disease eats away at their limbs. Death's firstborn devours their bodies.
They're torn from the safety of their tents and brought to the king of terrors.
What doesn't belong to them takes over their tents, and sulfur is scattered over their homes.
Their roots dry up below, and their branches are cut off above.
Their memory disappears from the earth. No one speaks their name in the street.
They're driven out of the light into darkness and chased out of the world.
They leave no child or grandchild among their people, no survivor where they lived.
People who come after them are appalled at their fate, just as those who came before them shuddered.
This is what becomes of the homes of the unrighteous. This is the place of someone who doesn't know God."
Then Job answered:
"How long will you torment me and crush me with your words?
You've insulted me ten times and aren't ashamed to keep attacking me.
If I really have gone wrong, my mistake is mine to bear.
If you're going to set yourselves above me and use my disgrace as evidence against me,
know this: God has wronged me and caught me in his net.
I cry out, 'I've been wronged!' but nobody hears me. I call for help and get no justice.
He's put a wall across my way so I can't get through and covered my paths with darkness.
He's stripped me of my honor and taken the crown off my head.
He's torn me down on every side until I'm finished. He's pulled up my hope like a tree.
He's kindled his anger against me and counts me as one of his enemies.
His troops come together, build a siege ramp against me, and camp around my tent.
He's driven my brothers far from me. The people who know me have become strangers.
My relatives have gone away, and my close friends have forgotten me.
The people staying in my house and my servant women treat me as a stranger. To them I'm an outsider.
I call my servant, but he doesn't answer, even when I beg him myself.
My breath offends my wife, and my own mother's children can't stand me.
Even little children despise me. When I stand up, they speak against me.
My closest friends are repulsed by me. The people I loved have turned against me.
My bones cling to my skin and flesh. I've escaped by the skin of my teeth.
Have pity on me, my friends. Have pity, because God's hand has struck me.
Why do you hound me as God does? Haven't you had enough of tearing at my flesh?
If only my words were written down! If only they were recorded in a book!
If only they were cut into rock forever with an iron tool and filled with lead!
But I know my Redeemer lives. In the end he'll stand upon the earth.
After my skin has been destroyed, I'll see God in my flesh.
I'll see him myself, on my side. My own eyes will see him. I won't be a stranger to him. My heart is spent within me.
If you say, 'How can we keep hounding him?' because you think the root of the problem is in me,
you should fear the sword. Anger brings the punishment of the sword, so you'll know there is a judgment."
Then Zophar the Naamathite answered:
"My thoughts are pressing me to answer. I feel an urgent need to speak.
I've heard a rebuke that shames me, and my understanding gives me a reply.
Don't you know how it's been from long ago, ever since humanity was placed on the earth?
The triumph of the wicked is brief, and the joy of the godless lasts only a moment.
Even if someone rises as high as heaven and their head touches the clouds,
they'll disappear forever like their own dung. People who saw them will ask, 'Where did they go?'
They'll vanish like a dream and won't be found, swept away like a vision in the night.
The eyes that saw them won't see them again. Their own place won't see them anymore.
Their children will have to seek the favor of the poor, and they'll have to give their wealth back with their own hands.
Their bones may be full of youthful strength, but that strength will lie down with them in the dust.
Wickedness may taste sweet in their mouth, and they may hide it under their tongue,
holding on to it and keeping it in their mouth as long as they can.
But the food turns sour inside them. It becomes cobra venom in their belly.
They swallow riches and vomit them back up. God forces the wealth out of them.
They suck in cobra venom, and the viper's tongue kills them.
They'll never gaze on the streams, the rivers flowing with honey and butter.
They'll have to give back what they worked for without swallowing it down. They won't enjoy the wealth they acquired.
They oppressed the poor and left them helpless. They seized houses they had no part in building.
Because their appetite never let them rest, they won't save any of the things they crave.
They left nothing they hadn't devoured, so their prosperity won't last.
At the height of their abundance, distress will overtake them. The hand of everyone in misery will come against them.
Just as they're about to fill their belly, God will rain down his fierce anger on them as they eat.
They may run from an iron weapon, only to be pierced by a bronze arrow.
They pull it out of their body, the gleaming point from their liver, and terrors fall on them.
Darkness is stored up for their treasures. A fire no one fanned will devour them and consume all that's left in their tent.
Heaven will expose their guilt, and the earth will rise against them.
Everything in their house will be swept away, carried off in the day of God's anger.
This is what God gives the wicked. It's the inheritance he has appointed for them."
Then Job answered:
"Listen closely to what I say. If you want to comfort me, start by listening.
Give me a chance to speak. After I've finished, you can go back to mocking me.
Is my complaint against a human being? Why shouldn't I be impatient?
Look at me and be appalled. Put your hand over your mouth.
When I think about it, I'm shaken, and my whole body trembles with horror.
Why do wicked people live on, grow old, and gain power?
They see their children firmly established around them, their descendants right in front of them.
Their homes are safe from fear, and God's rod never strikes them.
Their bulls breed without fail. Their cows give birth without miscarrying.
They send their little ones out like a flock, and their children dance.
They sing to the tambourine and harp and celebrate to the sound of the flute.
They live out their days in prosperity and go down to Sheol in an instant.
Yet they tell God, 'Leave us alone. We don't want to know your ways.
Who is the Almighty that we should serve him? What would we gain by praying to him?'
Their prosperity is beyond their own control. I want nothing to do with the plans of the wicked.
How often does the lamp of the wicked actually go out? How often does disaster overtake them, or God deal out suffering in his anger?
How often are they like straw before the wind, like chaff swept away in a storm?
You say, 'God saves up the punishment for their children.' Let him repay the wrongdoer directly so they know what they've done.
Let their own eyes see their destruction. Let them drink the anger of the Almighty.
What do they care what happens to their household after them, once their allotted months are cut short?
Can anyone teach God anything, when he judges even those in the highest places?
One person dies in full strength, completely comfortable and at peace.
Their pails are full of milk, and the marrow in their bones is moist.
Another dies bitter at heart, having never tasted anything good.
They lie down side by side in the dust, and worms cover them both.
I know what you're thinking and what you're plotting to do to me.
You ask, 'Where is the ruler's house now? Where is the tent where the wicked lived?'
Haven't you asked people who travel the roads? Don't you know what they've seen,
that an evil person is kept for the day of disaster and led away on the day of wrath?
Who confronts them about their conduct? Who repays them for what they've done?
Even so, they're carried to the grave, and people keep watch over their tomb.
The soil of the valley lies sweet upon them. A crowd follows after them, just as countless people went before them.
How can you comfort me with nonsense when all that's left of your answers is falsehood?"
Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered:
"Can a person be of any use to God? Even the wise benefit only themselves.
Does the Almighty gain any pleasure from your being righteous? Does he benefit if your conduct is blameless?
Is it because you revere him that he rebukes you and brings you into court?
Isn't your wickedness great? There's no end to the wrongs you've done.
You took security from your own people for no reason and stripped people of what little clothing they had.
You gave no water to the weary and kept bread away from the hungry.
The powerful owned the land, and the privileged settled in it.
You sent widows away empty-handed and broke the strength of the fatherless.
That's why traps surround you and sudden fear overwhelms you,
why darkness leaves you unable to see and floodwaters cover you.
Isn't God in the heights of heaven? Look at the stars and see how high they are.
Yet you say, 'What does God know? Can he judge through thick darkness?
Heavy clouds cover him so he can't see. He walks above the vault of the sky.'
Will you stay on the old path that wicked people walked?
They were swept away before their time, their foundations washed away like a stream.
They said to God, 'Leave us alone! What can the Almighty do for us?'
Yet he filled their homes with good things. I want nothing to do with the schemes of wicked people.
The righteous see their downfall and rejoice, and the innocent laugh at them.
They say, 'Our enemies have been cut off, and fire has burned up what they left behind.'
Get to know God and be at peace with him. Good will come to you through that.
Please accept instruction from his mouth and keep his words in your heart.
If you return to the Almighty and put injustice far from your tents, you'll be built up again.
Lay your treasure in the dust and your gold from Ophir among the stones of the streambed.
Then the Almighty will be your treasure and your precious silver.
You'll delight in the Almighty and lift your face to God.
You'll pray to him, and he'll hear you. You'll make good on your vows.
You'll decide on something, and it will succeed for you. Light will shine on your paths.
When people are brought low, you'll ask for them to be lifted up, and God will save the humble.
He'll even rescue someone who isn't innocent. They'll be rescued through the cleanness of your hands."
Then Job answered:
"Even today my complaint sounds rebellious. His hand weighs heavily on me despite my groaning.
If only I knew where to find him! Then I could go straight to his seat.
I'd lay out my case before him and have my arguments ready.
I'd find out what he'd say in reply and understand what he told me.
Would he argue against me with all his power? No, he'd listen to me.
There an upright person could reason with him, and I'd be acquitted by my judge for good.
If I go east, he's nowhere to be found. If I go west, I can't find him.
When he's at work in the north, I can't see him. He turns south, and I can't catch a glimpse of him.
But he knows the path I'm taking. When he's tested me, I'll come out like gold.
My feet have followed his steps closely. I've stayed on his path without turning away.
I haven't turned back from what he commanded. I've treasured his words more than the food I need.
He stands alone. Who can stand against him? He does whatever he desires.
He carries out what he's appointed for me, and he has many more things like that in store.
That's why I'm terrified in his presence. The more I think about it, the more I fear him.
God has made me lose heart. The Almighty has terrified me.
I wasn't cut off before the darkness came, and he hasn't hidden the thick darkness from my face."
"Why doesn't the Almighty set times for judgment? Why don't those who know him get to see those days?
People move boundary stones and steal flocks, then graze the animals as their own.
They drive off the orphans' donkey and take the widow's ox as security for a debt.
They push the needy off the road, and the poor of the land all go into hiding.
Like wild donkeys in the desert, the poor go out to work, searching hard for food. The wilderness provides bread for their children.
They cut what they can eat in the fields and gather leftovers in the vineyards of the wicked.
They spend the night naked, with no clothes and nothing to cover themselves in the cold.
They're soaked by mountain showers and cling to the rocks because they have no shelter.
Some people tear a fatherless child from the breast and take what little the poor have as security for a debt.
The poor go around naked, without clothing, and they carry bundles of grain while going hungry.
They press oil between their oppressors' walls and tread their winepresses while going thirsty.
People groan in the crowded city, and the wounded cry for help, yet God pays no attention to the wrongdoing.
There are people who rebel against the light. They don't know its ways or stay on its paths.
The murderer gets up at daylight and kills the poor and needy. At night he acts like a thief.
The adulterer watches for dusk, thinking, 'No one will see me,' and covers his face.
In the dark they break into houses, and by day they shut themselves inside. They want nothing to do with the light.
Morning is like deep darkness to them, because they're at home with the terrors of the dark.
They're like foam on the surface of the water. Their share of the land is cursed, and they no longer go down the path to the vineyards.
As drought and heat swallow up the melted snow, Sheol swallows up those who've sinned.
Even the womb that bore them forgets them. Worms feast on them, and no one remembers them anymore. Wrongdoing is snapped like a tree.
They prey on women who have no children and show no kindness to widows.
Yet God keeps the powerful alive by his strength. They get up again when they have no assurance of life.
God gives them security, and they rest in it, while his eyes watch what they do.
They're lifted high for a little while, then they're gone. They're brought low and taken away like everyone else, cut off like the heads of grain.
If that isn't true, who can prove I'm lying and show that my words are worthless?"
Then Bildad the Shuhite answered:
"Rule and awe belong to God. He makes peace in the heights of heaven.
Can anyone count his armies? Is there anyone his light doesn't shine on?
How can a person be in the right before God? How can anyone born of a woman be clean?
Look, even the moon isn't bright in his eyes, and the stars aren't pure to him.
How much less a mortal, who is only a maggot, a human being, who is only a worm!"
Then Job answered:
"What a help you've been to someone who has no power! What a rescue for an arm with no strength!
What advice you've given to someone without wisdom! How much sound knowledge you've shared!
Who were you speaking to? Whose spirit spoke through you?
The spirits of the dead tremble beneath the waters and all that live in them.
Sheol lies bare before God, and Abaddon has nothing to cover it.
He stretches the northern skies over empty space and hangs the earth on nothing.
He wraps the waters in thick clouds, yet the clouds don't burst under their weight.
He covers the face of his throne and spreads his cloud over it.
He draws a boundary on the surface of the waters where light meets darkness.
The pillars of heaven tremble and stand in shock at his rebuke.
By his power he stirs up the sea, and by his understanding he strikes down Rahab.
His Spirit makes the heavens beautiful. His hand pierces the swift serpent.
And these are only the edges of what he does. We hear so faint a whisper of him. Who can understand the thunder of his power?"
Job continued his speech:
"As surely as God lives, the God who has denied me justice, the Almighty who has made my life bitter,
as long as I still have breath in me and God's breath is in my nostrils,
my lips will speak no wrong and my tongue will tell no lies.
I'll never say that you are right. I will hold on to my integrity until the day I die.
I hold on to my righteousness and won't let go. My conscience won't accuse me as long as I live.
May my enemy meet the fate of the wicked, and may anyone who rises against me end up like the unjust.
What hope do the godless have when they're cut off, when God takes their life?
Will God hear their cry when trouble overtakes them?
Will they take delight in the Almighty and call on God at all times?
I'll teach you what God's hand can do. I won't hide what the Almighty has in store.
You've all seen it yourselves, so why keep talking nonsense?
This is what God gives the wicked, the inheritance oppressors receive from the Almighty.
No matter how many children they have, the sword waits for them, and their descendants will never have enough bread.
Those who survive them will be carried to their graves, and their widows won't mourn.
They may heap up silver like dust and pile up clothes like dirt.
They may pile it all up, but the righteous will wear the clothes and the innocent will divide the silver.
They build houses as fragile as a moth's shelter, like a temporary hut a watchman sets up.
They lie down rich, but never will again. When they open their eyes, everything is gone.
Terrors overtake them like floodwaters. A storm carries them off in the night.
The east wind lifts them away, and they're gone. It sweeps them out of their home.
It hurls itself at them without pity as they try to escape its grip.
People clap at their downfall and hiss them out of their home."
There are mines for silver and places where people refine gold.
People dig iron out of the ground and melt copper out of its ore.
They bring light into the darkness and search as far as they can for stone buried in deep shadows.
They sink a shaft far from where people live, where no one passes by. Far from everyone, they hang and swing back and forth.
Food grows from the earth above, while underneath it the ground is torn up as if by fire.
Its rocks hold sapphires, and there is gold dust down there.
No bird of prey knows that path. Even a falcon has never spotted it.
Proud beasts have never set foot there. Even the fiercest lion has never passed that way.
People break through hard rock and overturn mountains at their roots.
They cut channels through the rock and spot every precious thing.
They dam up streams to stop the water from seeping in, and bring hidden things to light.
But where can you find wisdom? Where does understanding live?
No one knows what wisdom is worth. It cannot be found in the land of the living.
The deep says, ‘It isn’t in me.’ The sea says, ‘I don’t have it.’
You can’t buy it with gold or weigh out enough silver to pay for it.
Even the gold of Ophir, precious onyx, and sapphire can’t match its value.
Gold and glass can’t compare to it. You can’t trade fine gold jewelry for it.
Coral and crystal aren’t even worth mentioning. Wisdom is worth more than rubies.
Topaz from Ethiopia can’t compare. Even pure gold can’t measure its worth.
So where does wisdom come from? Where does understanding live?
It’s hidden from every living eye, even from the birds overhead.
Destruction and Death say, ‘We’ve only heard rumors about it.’
God knows the way to wisdom. He knows where it lives.
He can see to the ends of the earth. He sees everything under the sky.
He set the force of the wind and measured out the waters.
He set a rule for the rain and marked out a path for the thunderbolt.
Then he saw wisdom and declared it. He established it and examined it thoroughly.
He told humanity, ‘To fear the Lord is wisdom. To turn away from evil is understanding.’
Job went on with his speech:
I wish I could go back to those earlier months, to the days when God watched over me.
His lamp shone over my head, and by his light I walked through the dark.
I was in my prime, and God’s friendship filled my tent.
The Almighty was still with me then, and my children were all around me.
My path flowed with butter, and even the rock poured out streams of oil for me.
I used to go to the city gate and take my seat in the public square.
The young men saw me and stepped out of sight. The elders got up and stood.
The leaders stopped talking and put their hands over their mouths.
The nobles fell quiet. Their tongues stuck to the roofs of their mouths.
Everyone who heard me blessed me, and everyone who saw me spoke well of me.
I rescued the poor who cried for help and the fatherless who had no one to stand up for them.
People who were close to dying blessed me, and I made widows sing for joy.
I wore righteousness like clothing. Justice was my robe and my crown.
I was eyes for the blind and feet for those who couldn’t walk.
I was a father to those in need, and I looked into the case of someone I didn’t even know.
I broke the jaws of the wicked and snatched their prey right out of their teeth.
I thought, ‘I’ll die in my own home, with days as countless as grains of sand.
My roots reach the water, and dew settles on my branches all night.
My honor stays fresh, and my bow is always strong in my hand.’
People listened to me and waited in silence for my advice.
After I spoke, no one had anything to add. My words sank in.
They waited for my words like people waiting for rain, taking them in like spring showers.
I smiled at them when they were losing heart, and they welcomed the light on my face.
I showed them which way to go and sat among them as their leader. I lived like a king among his troops and comforted people who were grieving.
But now men younger than me laugh at me, men whose fathers I wouldn’t even have put with my sheepdogs.
What good was their strength to me? Their vigor had already worn away.
Starving and gaunt, they gnaw at the dry ground in the gloom of a desolate wasteland.
They pick salty plants by the bushes and eat the roots of broom trees.
People drive them out and shout after them as if they were thieves.
They live in frightening ravines, in holes in the ground and in the rocks.
They bray among the bushes and huddle beneath the nettles.
They are children of fools and of the wicked, whipped out of the land.
Now they make songs about me. My name has become a joke to them.
They can’t stand me. They keep their distance and think nothing of spitting in my face.
God loosened his cord and brought me low, and now they hold nothing back around me.
A mob rises up at my right. They knock my feet out from under me and pile up ramps to attack me.
They tear up my path and push me toward ruin without anyone’s help.
They surge in as if through a wide gap in a wall, rolling in through the wreckage.
Terrors close in on me. They sweep my honor away like the wind, and my well-being vanishes like a cloud.
Now my life is draining away. Days of suffering have taken hold of me.
At night my bones feel pierced, and the pain that gnaws at me never lets up.
A great force twists my clothes and grips me like the collar of my tunic.
God has thrown me into the mud. I’ve become like dust and ashes.
I cry out to you, but you don’t answer. I stand up, and you just look at me.
You’ve turned cruel toward me. With all your strength you come after me.
You lift me into the wind and drive me along with it. You toss me until I fall apart in the storm.
I know you’ll bring me to death, the home set aside for everyone who lives.
Doesn’t a person reach out a hand when they fall? Don’t they cry for help when disaster strikes?
Didn’t I cry for people in trouble? Didn’t my heart ache for those in need?
I looked for good, but trouble came. I waited for light, but darkness came.
My heart churns and can’t settle down. Days of suffering have come for me.
I walk around in mourning, with no sunlight. I stand up in the assembly and cry for help.
I’ve become a brother to jackals and a companion to ostriches.
My skin darkens and peels, and my bones burn with heat.
My harp now plays songs of mourning, and my flute sounds like people weeping.
I made a covenant with my eyes. How could I look at a young woman with lust?
What share would God above give me? What would I inherit from the Almighty on high?
Doesn’t ruin fall on the unrighteous and disaster on people who do wrong?
Doesn’t God see how I live and count every step I take?
If I’ve lived a lie or rushed to deceive anyone,
let God weigh me on honest scales so he can see my integrity.
If I’ve strayed from the right path, let my heart chase what my eyes wanted, or let any wrongdoing stick to my hands,
then let someone else eat what I plant, and let my crops be pulled up by the roots.
If another woman has drawn my heart away and I’ve waited in secret at my neighbor’s door,
then let my wife grind grain for another man, and let other men sleep with her.
That would be a shameful crime, an offense for judges to punish.
It would be a fire that burns everything to ruin and uproots all I’ve gained.
If I brushed aside the complaint of a man or woman who worked for me when they brought a case against me,
what would I do when God rises to judge? What could I say when he calls me to account?
Didn’t the same God who made me in the womb make them too? Didn’t one God form us both?
If I kept the poor from getting what they needed or made a widow lose hope,
or if I ate my food alone and gave none to the fatherless,
though since my youth I raised the fatherless like a father and guided widows from my earliest days,
if I saw anyone dying for lack of clothes or saw a needy person with nothing to wear,
and they had no reason to bless me because I never warmed them with the wool from my sheep,
or if I raised my hand against the fatherless because I knew I had allies at the city gate,
then let my shoulder come out of its socket and my arm snap at the joint.
Disaster from God terrifies me. Before his majesty I can do nothing.
If I put my hope in gold and told pure gold, ‘You’re what I count on,’
if I took pride in how rich I was and how much I’d gained by my own hand,
if I saw the sun shining or the moon moving in splendor,
and my heart was secretly drawn to them and I blew them a kiss,
that too would be an offense for judges to punish, because I would have denied God above.
If I celebrated when someone who hated me was ruined or gloated when trouble found them,
though I never let my mouth sin by cursing them and asking for their life,
or if the people in my tent couldn’t say, ‘Can you find anyone who hasn’t had their fill of his food?’
though I opened my doors to travelers so strangers didn’t have to sleep in the street,
if I covered up my wrongs like Adam and hid my guilt in my heart,
because I was afraid of the crowd and terrified of what families might think, so I stayed quiet and never went outside,
if only someone would hear me! Here’s my signature. Let the Almighty answer me. Let my accuser write down the charges!
I’d carry that document on my shoulder and wear it like a crown.
I’d account for every step I’ve taken. I’d approach him like a prince.
If my land cries out against me and its furrows weep together,
if I’ve eaten what it produced without paying or caused its owners to lose their lives,
then let thornbushes grow instead of wheat and stinkweed instead of barley. Job’s words end here.
The three men stopped answering Job because he was convinced he was in the right.
Then Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite, from the family of Ram, got angry with Job for defending himself instead of defending God.
He was also angry with Job’s three friends because they had condemned Job even though they had found no answer for him.
Elihu had waited to speak to Job because the others were older than he was.
When Elihu saw that the three men had nothing left to say, he got angry.
Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite said, “I’m young, and you’re much older. So I held back and didn’t dare tell you what I thought.
I thought, ‘Age should have its say. A long life should teach wisdom.’
But it’s the spirit in a person, the breath of the Almighty, that gives understanding.
Being important doesn’t make a person wise, and being old doesn’t guarantee they understand justice.
So I said, ‘Listen to me. I’ll tell you what I think too.’
I waited to hear what you had to say. I listened to your reasoning as you searched for the right words.
I gave you my full attention. None of you proved Job wrong or answered what he said.
Don’t say, ‘We’ve found wisdom. Only God can prove him wrong.’
Job hasn’t aimed his words at me, and I won’t answer him with the speeches you gave.
They’re stunned and have stopped answering. They don’t have a word to say.
Should I keep waiting because they won’t speak, because they just stand there with no answer?
I’ll give my own answer and say what I think.
I have plenty to say, and the spirit inside me won’t let me hold it in.
I feel like wine sealed tight in a new wineskin that’s about to burst.
I need to speak to get some relief. I’ll open my mouth and answer.
I won’t play favorites or flatter anyone with fancy titles.
I wouldn’t know how to flatter someone. If I did, my Maker would soon take me away.
Job, please hear me out and listen to everything I have to say.
I’ve opened my mouth, and I’m ready to speak.
I’ll speak honestly from my heart and tell you sincerely what I know.
The Spirit of God made me, and the breath of the Almighty gives me life.
Answer me if you can. Get your words in order and take your stand.
I’m just like you before God. I too was shaped from clay.
You have no reason to be afraid of me. I won’t put any heavy pressure on you.
I heard you speak. These are the words I heard you say:
‘I’m clean and haven’t rebelled. I’m innocent, and there’s no wrongdoing in me.
Yet God finds reasons to accuse me. He treats me like his enemy.
He locks my feet in stocks and watches every path I take.’
Here’s my answer. You’re wrong about this, because God is greater than any human.
Why do you argue with him over his refusal to explain what he does?
God speaks once and then again, though people pay no attention.
He speaks in a dream, in a vision at night, when people are in a deep sleep on their beds.
Then he opens their ears and makes sure his warning sinks in.
He wants to turn them away from what they were set on doing and keep them from pride.
He keeps them from going down to the pit and saves their lives from the sword.
A person can also be corrected through pain in bed, with an endless ache in their bones.
They can’t stand the thought of bread. Even their favorite food makes them sick.
They waste away until there’s nothing left of their flesh, and bones that used to be hidden stick out.
Their life comes close to the pit, and they draw near to those who bring death.
But there may be an angel at their side, a messenger one in a thousand, to show them what is right for them.
Then God has mercy and says, ‘Keep them from going down to the pit. I’ve found a ransom.’
Their flesh will be fresher than a child’s, and they’ll regain the strength of their youth.
They pray to God, and he welcomes them. They see his face with joy, and he restores them to a right standing.
They sing in front of others, ‘I sinned and twisted what was right, and I gained nothing from it.
God saved me from going down to the pit. Now I’ll live to see the light.’
God does all this for a person twice and even three times,
to bring them back from the pit so the light of the living can shine on them.
Pay attention, Job, and listen to me. Stay quiet and let me speak.
If you have something to say, answer me. Speak up, because I want to see you cleared.
Otherwise, listen to me. Be quiet, and I’ll teach you wisdom.”
Elihu went on:
Listen to what I’m saying, you wise men. Hear me out, you who have knowledge.
The ear tests words the way the tongue tastes food.
Let’s decide for ourselves what’s right and work out together what’s good.
Job has said, ‘I’m in the right, but God has denied me justice.
Even though I’m right, I’m treated as a liar. My wound won’t heal, though I haven’t rebelled.’
Who is like Job? He drinks up scorn like water.
He keeps company with people who do wrong and walks with the wicked.
He’s said, ‘What good does it do anyone to take delight in God?’
So listen to me, you who have understanding. It’s unthinkable for God to do evil or for the Almighty to do wrong.
He pays people back for what they’ve done and gives each person what their conduct deserves.
God will never do evil. The Almighty will never twist justice.
Who put him in charge of the earth? Who appointed him over the whole world?
If he turned his attention only to himself and took back his spirit and his breath,
every living thing would die together, and human beings would return to dust.
If you have understanding, hear this. Listen to what I’m saying.
Should someone who hates justice be in charge? Will you condemn the one who is righteous and mighty,
who can say to a king, ‘You’re vile,’ and to nobles, ‘You’re wicked’?
He doesn’t favor rulers or give the rich special treatment over the poor. He made them all with his own hands.
They can die in an instant, even at midnight. People are shaken and pass away. The mighty are swept away without a human hand.
God watches how people live. He sees every step they take.
There’s no darkness or deep shadow where people who do wrong can hide.
God doesn’t need to examine anyone further before calling them before him for judgment.
He shatters the mighty in ways no one can trace and puts others in their place.
He knows what they’ve done. He overturns them in the night, and they are crushed.
He strikes them in public for the evil they’ve done,
because they turned away from him and refused to pay attention to his ways.
They made the poor cry out to him, and he heard the cries of people who were suffering.
If God grants peace, who can condemn him? If he hides his face, who can see him? He rules over nations and individuals alike,
to keep godless people from ruling and laying traps for others.
Has anyone said to God, ‘I’m guilty, and I’ll stop doing wrong.
Teach me what I can’t see. If I’ve done wrong, I won’t do it again’?
Should God repay you on your terms just because you reject his decision? The choice is yours. Tell me what you know.
People with understanding will tell me, and so will every wise person who hears me,
‘Job speaks without knowledge. There’s no wisdom in his words.’
I wish Job’s claims were tested all the way, because he answers like people who do evil.
He adds rebellion to his sin. He claps his hands in front of us and keeps piling up words against God.
Elihu continued:
Do you think you’re right to say, ‘I’m more righteous than God,’
and then ask, ‘What good does it do you? What do I gain by keeping from sin?’
I’ll answer you and your friends with you.
Look up at the sky. See how high the clouds are above you.
If you sin, how does that harm God? If you keep piling up wrongs, what does that do to him?
If you do what is right, what do you give him? What does he receive from your hand?
Your wickedness can hurt someone like you, and your righteousness can help another person.
People cry out under all kinds of oppression. They call for help against the power of the mighty.
But no one asks, ‘Where is God, my Maker, who gives songs in the night,
who teaches us more than the animals on earth and makes us wiser than the birds in the sky?’
They cry out, but no one answers, because of the pride of evil people.
God won’t listen to an empty cry. The Almighty won’t pay attention to it.
How much less when you say you can’t see him! Your case is already before him, so wait for him.
But for now God hasn’t punished in anger or paid much attention to arrogance,
so Job opens his mouth and says nothing of substance. He piles up words without knowing what he’s talking about.
Elihu went on:
Bear with me a little longer and I’ll explain. I still have something to say on God’s behalf.
I’ll draw on knowledge from far away and show that my Maker does what is right.
What I’m telling you is true. Someone with complete knowledge is here with you.
Look, God is mighty, yet he looks down on no one. His understanding is as great as his strength.
He doesn’t keep the wicked alive, but he gives justice to those who suffer.
He keeps his eyes on the righteous. He seats them with kings on their thrones and lifts them up forever.
If they are bound in chains and caught in the ropes of suffering,
he shows them what they’ve done wrong and how proudly they’ve acted.
He opens their ears to correction and tells them to turn away from wrongdoing.
If they listen and serve him, they’ll live out their days in prosperity and their years in joy.
But if they refuse to listen, they’ll die by the sword without ever understanding.
People whose hearts turn away from God store up anger. They don’t cry for help when he binds them.
They die young, and their lives end among the unclean.
God rescues suffering people through their suffering. He gets their attention in the middle of their oppression.
He would have drawn you out of trouble into a wide-open place where nothing could hem you in. Your table would have been loaded with rich food.
But now you’re weighed down with the judgment that falls on the wicked. Judgment and justice have taken hold of you.
Watch out that wealth doesn’t lure you into anger or a big bribe turn you aside.
Could your wealth or all your strength keep you going when trouble comes?
Don’t long for the night, when people are cut off where they stand.
Be careful to stay away from wrongdoing. You’ve chosen it over suffering.
God is exalted in his power. Who teaches like he does?
Who has told him what to do? Who can say to him, ‘You’ve done wrong’?
Remember to praise what he’s done, the work people have sung about.
Everyone has looked at it. People can see it from far away.
God is great beyond what we can know. No one can count his years.
He draws up drops of water, and the vapor condenses into rain.
The clouds pour it out, and it falls on people in abundance.
Can anyone understand how the clouds spread or how thunder rolls from his shelter?
Look how he spreads his light all around him. He covers the depths of the sea.
By these things he judges the peoples and gives them plenty of food.
He fills his hands with lightning and tells it where to strike.
The thunder announces him, and the cattle sense the storm coming.
At this my heart trembles and feels like it might leap out of my chest.
Listen closely to the rumble of God’s voice, the sound that comes from his mouth.
He sends it across the whole sky and sends his lightning to the ends of the earth.
Then comes the roar. He thunders with a majestic voice and holds nothing back when it is heard.
God’s voice thunders in ways that fill us with wonder. He does great things we can’t understand.
He tells the snow, ‘Fall on the earth,’ and gives the same command to the rain, even to the heaviest downpour.
He brings everyone’s work to a stop so the people he made can see what he’s doing.
The animals take shelter and stay in their dens.
The storm comes out of its chamber, and the cold comes from the north.
God breathes out and ice forms. Even broad stretches of water freeze over.
He loads the thick clouds with moisture and spreads out the clouds that flash with his lightning.
He steers them wherever he wants, so they do what he commands across the inhabited world.
He sends them to correct people, to care for his land, or to show his faithful love.
Listen to this, Job. Stand still and think about the wonders God does.
Do you know how God directs the clouds and makes lightning flash from them?
Do you know how the clouds work? These are the wonders of the one whose knowledge is complete.
Do you know why your clothes feel so warm when the south wind leaves the land still?
Can you help him spread out the sky, as hard as a mirror cast from metal?
Tell us what we should say to him. We’re in the dark and can’t put our case together.
Should he be told that I want to speak? Would anyone ask to be swallowed up?
People can’t see the bright light in the sky until the wind blows through and clears it.
Golden splendor comes out of the north. God is clothed in awe-inspiring majesty.
We can’t reach the Almighty. His power is beyond us, and with all his justice and righteousness he never oppresses anyone.
That’s why people revere him. He pays no special attention to those who think themselves wise.
Then the LORD answered Job from the whirlwind:
Who is this, clouding my counsel with words spoken without knowledge?
Brace yourself like a man. I’ll ask the questions, and you’ll answer me.
Where were you when I laid the earth’s foundations? Tell me, if you understand.
Who set its dimensions, if you know? Who stretched a measuring line across it?
What holds its foundations in place? Who set its cornerstone
while the morning stars sang together and all the sons of God shouted for joy?
Who shut the sea behind doors when it burst out of the womb,
when I dressed it in clouds and wrapped it in thick darkness,
when I marked its boundary and put doors and bars in place,
and said, ‘You can come this far and no farther. This is where your proud waves stop’?
Have you ever given orders to the morning or shown the dawn where to rise,
so it could grab the earth by its edges and shake the wicked out of it?
The earth takes shape like clay beneath a seal, and its features stand out like folds in a garment.
The wicked lose their light, and their raised arm is broken.
Have you gone down to the springs of the sea or walked through the hidden depths?
Have the gates of death been shown to you? Have you seen the gates of death’s shadow?
Have you taken in the full width of the earth? Tell me if you know all of it.
Which way leads to where light lives? And where does darkness live,
so you could take each one home and find the paths to where they belong?
Of course you know! You were already born back then, and you’ve lived for so many years!
Have you entered the storehouses of snow or seen where I keep the hail,
which I hold in reserve for times of trouble, for the day of battle and war?
Which way does lightning spread, and how does the east wind scatter over the earth?
Who dug a channel for the floodwaters and made a path for thunderstorms,
to send rain on land where no one lives, on wilderness with no people,
to soak the empty wasteland and make new grass sprout?
Does rain have a father? Who fathers the drops of dew?
From whose womb did ice come? Who gave birth to the gray frost from the sky?
Water turns hard as stone when the surface of the deep freezes over.
Can you tie the stars of the Pleiades together or untie Orion’s cords?
Can you bring the constellations out in their seasons or guide the Bear with her cubs?
Do you know the laws of the heavens? Can you make those laws govern the earth?
Can you call up to the clouds so a flood of water comes down over you?
Can you send lightning on its way? Does it report back to you, ‘Here we are’?
Who put wisdom deep inside people? Who gave the mind understanding?
Who is wise enough to count the clouds or tip over the water jars of the sky,
when the dust packs together and the lumps of earth stick to one another?
Can you hunt for the lioness or feed her hungry young
when they crouch in their dens or lie in wait in the brush?
Who finds food for the ravens when their young cry out to God and wander because they have nothing to eat?
Do you know when the mountain goats give birth? Have you watched a doe give birth to her fawns?
Can you count the months they carry their young? Do you know when they’ll give birth?
They crouch down, deliver their young, and their labor pains end.
Their young grow strong in the open country. They go out on their own and never return.
Who let the wild donkey go free? Who untied the ropes of that swift donkey?
I gave him the wilderness for a home and the salt flats as a place to live.
He laughs at the noise of the city and never hears a driver shouting at him.
The mountains are his pasture, and he searches for every green thing he can find.
Will the wild ox agree to work for you? Will it spend the night by your feeding trough?
Can you harness it to plow a straight furrow? Will it follow you and till the valleys?
Will you trust it because it’s so strong and leave it to do your work?
Can you count on it to bring in what you’ve sown and gather grain at your threshing floor?
The ostrich flaps her wings proudly, but do those feathers show any tenderness?
She leaves her eggs on the ground and lets them warm in the dust.
She forgets that a foot could crush them or that a wild animal could trample them.
