She treats her young harshly, as though they weren’t hers. She doesn’t worry that her labor might go to waste,
because God withheld wisdom from her and gave her no understanding.
But when she rises to run, she laughs at the horse and its rider.
Did you give the horse its strength? Did you dress its neck with a rippling mane?
Did you teach it to leap like a locust? Its mighty snort fills people with awe.
It paws the ground in the valley, eager to use its strength, and charges toward armed men.
It laughs at fear and doesn’t flinch or turn away from the sword.
The quiver rattles at its side along with the flashing spear and javelin.
It tears across the ground in a fury and won’t stand still when the trumpet sounds.
At each blast it snorts, ‘Aha!’ It smells battle far away and hears the commanders thundering and the soldiers shouting.
Is it your wisdom that makes the hawk soar and spread its wings toward the south?
Does the eagle rise at your command and build its nest high above the ground?
It lives on the cliff and makes its home on a rocky ledge, safe in its stronghold.
From there it watches for prey, spotting it from far away.
Its young drink blood. Wherever the dead lie, the eagle is there.
The LORD went on speaking to Job:
Will the one who disputes with the Almighty keep arguing? Let the one who challenges God give an answer.
Then Job answered the LORD:
I’m so small. What could I possibly say to you? I put my hand over my mouth.
I’ve spoken once, and I won’t answer again. I’ve spoken twice, and I won’t say any more.
Then the LORD answered Job from the whirlwind:
Now brace yourself like a man. I’ll ask the questions, and you’ll answer me.
Will you overturn my judgment? Will you condemn me so you can claim you’re in the right?
Is your arm as strong as God’s? Can your voice thunder like his?
Go ahead and clothe yourself with splendor and dignity. Put on honor and majesty.
Pour out the full force of your anger. Look at every proud person and bring them down.
Look at every proud person and humble them. Crush the wicked where they stand.
Bury them together in the dust. Bind their faces in that hidden place.
Then even I will admit that your own right hand can save you.
Look at Behemoth. I made him just as I made you. He eats grass like an ox.
Look at the strength in his thighs and the power in the muscles of his belly.
He swings his tail like a cedar. The tendons of his thighs are tightly woven together.
His bones are like bronze pipes, and his limbs are like bars of iron.
He ranks first among God’s works. The one who made him gives him his sword.
The mountains grow food for him, where all the wild animals play.
He lies under the lotus plants, hidden among the reeds in the marsh.
The lotus plants shade him, and the willows along the stream surround him.
When the river floods, he doesn’t flinch. He stays calm even if the Jordan rises to his mouth.
Can anyone catch him while he’s watching or pierce his nose with a snare?
Can you pull Leviathan out with a fishhook or tie down his tongue with a rope?
Can you run a rope through his nose or put a hook through his jaw?
Will he beg you over and over or speak softly to you?
Will he make a deal to serve you for the rest of his life?
Can you play with him like a pet bird or put him on a leash for your girls?
Will traders bargain over him and divide him among the merchants?
Can you cover his hide with barbed hooks or drive fishing spears into his head?
Just try laying a hand on him. You’ll remember the fight and never try again.
Any hope of catching him is useless. The sight of him alone is enough to bring you down.
No one is fierce enough to stir him up. So who can stand before me?
Who has ever given me anything that I owe them back? Everything under the sky is mine.
I won’t stay quiet about his limbs, his tremendous strength, or how well he’s built.
Who can strip off his outer armor? Who would dare come between his jaws?
Who can pry open the doors of his face? His teeth are terrifying from every side.
His rows of tough scales are his pride, sealed tightly together.
Each scale fits so close to the next that no air can pass between them.
They lock together so firmly that no one can pull them apart.
Light flashes when he sneezes, and his eyes gleam like the first light of dawn.
Burning torches shoot from his mouth, and sparks fly out.
Smoke pours from his nostrils like steam from a boiling pot over burning reeds.
His breath sets coals alight, and flames shoot from his mouth.
Strength fills his neck, and terror dances ahead of him.
The folds of his flesh fit together. They’re solid and won’t budge.
His heart is hard as stone, as hard as the lower millstone.
When he rises, even the mighty are afraid. They back away when he thrashes.
A sword can’t get through to him, and neither can a spear, a dart, or a pointed shaft.
Iron is like straw to him, and bronze is like rotten wood.
Arrows won’t drive him off. Sling stones are like husks blowing past him.
Clubs are just stubble to him, and he laughs when a javelin comes flying.
His belly is like sharp pieces of broken pottery, leaving tracks in the mud like a threshing sled.
He makes the deep churn like a boiling pot. He stirs the sea like ointment in a jar.
He leaves a shining trail behind him, as if the deep had turned white-haired.
There’s nothing on earth like him. He was made without fear.
He looks down on all that is lofty. He’s king over all who are proud.
Then Job answered the LORD:
I know you can do anything. Nothing can stop what you’ve decided to do.
You asked, ‘Who is this, hiding my counsel without knowledge?’ I spoke about things I didn’t understand, things too wonderful for me to know.
You said, ‘Listen now, and I’ll speak. I’ll ask the questions, and you’ll answer me.’
I had heard about you before, but now I see you with my own eyes.
So I reject what I said and repent in dust and ashes.
After the LORD finished speaking to Job, he said to Eliphaz the Temanite, “I’m angry with you and your two friends. You haven’t spoken rightly about me the way my servant Job has.

So take seven bulls and seven rams to my servant Job and offer them as a burnt offering for yourselves. My servant Job will pray for you, and I’ll accept his prayer, so I won’t deal with you as your foolishness deserves. You haven’t spoken rightly about me the way my servant Job has.”
So Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite did what the LORD told them, and the LORD accepted Job’s prayer.
When Job prayed for his friends, the LORD restored his prosperity and gave him twice as much as he’d had before.

All his brothers and sisters and everyone who’d known him before came and shared a meal at his house. They comforted him over all the suffering the LORD had brought on him. Each gave him a piece of money and a gold ring.
The LORD blessed the later years of Job’s life more than the early ones. Job had fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, a thousand pairs of oxen, and a thousand female donkeys.
He also had seven sons and three daughters.
He named his first daughter Jemimah, the second Keziah, and the third Keren Happuch.
Nowhere in the land were there women as beautiful as Job’s daughters. Their father gave them an inheritance alongside their brothers.
Job lived another hundred and forty years and saw his children and their descendants to the fourth generation.
Job died at a good old age, having lived a full life.
